newsitem.title: USA: U.S. patients to get more information on medicines.
newsitem.headline: U.S. patients to get more information on medicines.

text.p: People taking prescription drugs will get easy-to-read information about their medicine, including instructions on avoiding dangerous interactions with other drugs, under a new federal programme announced on Tuesay.

The programme, a collaboration between the government and private sector groups, aims to reduce the misuse of medicines that leads to thousands of hospitalizations every year. Under the plan, patients will receive information on how to take a medicine properly and on what to avoid.

Health officials distributed a sample leaflet for an antibiotic, Cefaclor, which explains that it is used to combat certain bacteria that cause middle ear, bladder and skin infections, as well as strep throat and pneumonia.
It goes on to warn patients about allergic reactions, side effects and what to do if a dose is missed, and says who should not take the medicine, such as nursing mothers.

The Food and Drug Administration in 1995 proposed developing and distributing medication guides that are easy to understand, scientifically accurate and not intended to promote a product. Congress opted to have the Department of Health and Human Services work with the private sector to develop a voluntary programme.

The programme was developed with participation by the drug industry and patient advocacy groups. The goal is to reach 75 percent of patients by 2000 and 95 percent by 2006. The FDA could take additional action if the voluntary approach fails.
